questions.q: Who was the founder of the Mauryan Empire, and who served as his main advisor?
questions.a: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire, and his advisor was Chanakya (also known as Kautilya). A wrong answer reveals the student is confusing the Mauryan period with other dynasties like the Nandas or later empires.

questions.q: In your own words, what was the biggest change in the Indian political landscape when the Mauryan Empire was established?
questions.a: The change was the move from many small, separate mahajanapadas to one large, unified empire under a single authority. A wrong answer shows the student does not understand the difference between a small kingdom and a vast empire.

questions.q: If Chandragupta Maurya wanted to add a neighboring land to his empire without starting a war, what method could he use?
questions.a: He could use diplomacy, such as making treaties or alliances with local rulers. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks conquest (war) is the only way empires grew, missing the role of negotiation.

questions.q: Why was the existence of mahajanapadas a challenge to creating a single, strong nation?
questions.a: Because mahajanapadas were independent kingdoms with their own kings, they likely competed with each other rather than working together. Understanding this helps students see why a strong, central leader was needed to bring them under one banner.

questions.q: Was the Mauryan Empire the very first group to settle in the Indian subcontinent? Defend your answer.
questions.a: No, the empire was formed long after the subcontinent was already populated and divided into mahajanapadas. This shows the student can differentiate between the *start of civilization* and the *start of an empire*.

questions.q: Imagine you are a leader in a small mahajanapada. If a massive empire like the Mauryan Empire approaches you, what are your options for survival?
questions.a: The student should suggest options like fighting, forming a diplomatic alliance, or surrendering to avoid destruction. A poor answer ignores the political reality of the time and fails to apply the concept of "conquest and diplomacy."
